title: Paper clay angel wing wall hanging
subtitle: A pair of textured relief wings pressed from paper clay and mounted as a wall piece
excerpt: These low-relief wings are pressed from paper-clay (air-dry) over a card template and dried flat. Feather detail is impressed with a real feather or a dental pick while the clay is still fresh. Mounted together on a painted board, they make a wall piece roughly 30 cm across. No kiln required.
sourceNotes: Paper clay slab and relief techniques derived from first principles. Wing motif form drawing on historic decorative plaster traditions; technique references derived from traditional hand-building methodology.

glossaryTerms.definition: A flat sheet of clay rolled to even thickness, usually between two wooden guide rails.
The drying stage where clay holds its shape but is still damp enough to texture and trim.
Air-dried but unfired clay. Fragile; the final stage before sealing an air-dry piece.

content.text: Paper clay has more structural integrity than standard air-dry clay because cellulose fibres knit the body together as it dries. This matters for a flat slab piece like a wall hanging: a plain air-dry
slab

of this size would bow as it dried; the paper fibres in paper-clay hold the panel flatter. The wing shapes are cut from rolled slabs using a card template, then textured with a real feather pressed into the surface while the clay is still fresh. The finished pieces are not waterproof: they mount indoors as decorative objects.
What you'll need

Approximately 500 g of paper-clay-air-dry. Two large feathers (from a craft supplier or naturally moulted: clean and dry before use). A card template: draw a wing shape roughly 14 cm long and 8 cm at the widest point. A flat board or tile to dry the wings on.
Rolling and cutting
Knead 500 g of paper-clay until uniform and smooth. Roll between 6 mm guide rails to produce a slab large enough for both wing shapes (roughly 30 × 20 cm).
Place the card template on the slab and cut around it with the fettling knife, holding the blade vertical. Flip the template and cut the mirror-image wing for the second piece.

Leave the slab in place: do not lift the wings yet. Press the feather, quill-side up, onto the wing surface. Rock a rolling pin gently over the feather to press it in uniformly to a depth of about 1 mm. Lift the feather straight up and off; do not drag it sideways or it smears the impression.
Once both wings are impressed, use the needle tool to draw individual barb lines radiating from the central quill impression. Work while the clay is still fresh for clean lines.
Pierce a hanging hole 5 mm from the top point of each wing with the needle tool.

Carefully slide the fettling knife under each wing and lift it onto a flat board for drying. If the wings curve slightly as they begin to stiffen, weight the edges gently with a light object (a rolled piece of card) until
leather-hard
Drying

Dry flat on the board for 48 hours. The paper fibres reduce bowing considerably but a long slab piece may still lift slightly at the corners: if this happens, press the corners gently flat while the clay is still leather-hard and weight them for another few hours. The pieces are
bone-dry
when they feel light and the colour is uniformly pale.
Finishing

Sand the edges lightly with 320-grit sandpaper. Apply a wash of thinned white acrylic paint to both surfaces, allowing it to settle into the impressed texture. Before it dries fully, wipe the raised surfaces with a dry cloth to remove the paint from the ridges and leave it concentrated in the grooves. This gives a depth effect: the feather barbs show darker than the raised clay between them.
When the paint is dry, apply two coats of acrylic sealant. Mount the wings side by side on a painted board or hang directly on a nail through the pierced holes.
Variations

Paper clay is stronger than plain air-dry clay. It has fibres inside that hold it flat as it dries. A plain air-dry slab this size would warp. Paper clay stays flat. Cut the wing shapes from rolled slabs using a card template. Press a real feather into the clay while it is fresh to add texture. The finished pieces are not waterproof. Mount them indoors.
Make the wings in grey or terracotta-coloured paper-clay and skip the white paint wash for a more muted, earthy finish.
Make three pairs in graduating sizes and mount them in a column for a more dramatic wall installation.

rows.cause: Surface dried faster than the underside; clay still too wet when lifted onto board
rows.fix: Let the slab reach leather-hard before lifting. Dry on a plaster bat if available: plaster absorbs moisture evenly from the underside.

rows.problem: Feather texture impression is faint or unclear
rows.cause: Rolling pin pressed unevenly; clay too dry when impressed
rows.fix: Impress immediately after cutting while the slab is still fresh. Press and roll firmly and evenly. Check the feather is clean and dry before pressing.

rows.cause: Clay too fragile after drying; walls too thin
rows.fix: Roll slabs at least 5 mm thick. Sand after sealing rather than before: the sealant binds the surface and reduces chipping.
